keyTakeaways: Dhanteras means 'the wealth thirteenth': dhan from Sanskrit dhana (wealth) and teras, the 13th lunar day (Platts, 1884, p. 351).
Dhanvantari's name comes from dhanvan, not dhana; Monier-Williams (1899) glosses it 'moving in a curve', and Gray (1922) called its meaning 'not wholly certain'.
The Yama lamp has the clearest written rule: one lamp outside the house at nightfall on the dark 13th 'to avoid accidental death' (Kane, 1958, pp. 195–196).
We found no text behind the popular King Hima story; it reads as a vrat katha that dramatises the Yama-lamp rule.
Ayurveda Day last fell on Dhanvantari Jayanti on 29 October 2024; since 2025 it is fixed on 23 September.

faqs.question: Why do we celebrate Dhanteras before Diwali?
faqs.answer: Dhanteras opens the five-day Diwali festival on the dark 13th of the lunar month, two days before Lakshmi Puja. It joins three observances on one evening: honouring wealth, worshipping Dhanvantari for health, and lighting a lamp outside the door for Yama to keep untimely death away.

faqs.question: What is the meaning of the word Dhanteras?
faqs.answer: It means the wealth thirteenth. Dhan comes from the Sanskrit dhana, wealth, and teras is the Hindi word for the 13th day of a lunar fortnight, which Platts's 1884 dictionary derives from Sanskrit trayodashi.

faqs.question: Is Dhanteras named after Lord Dhanvantari?
faqs.answer: Not according to the dictionaries. Monier-Williams splits Dhanvantari as dhanvan-tari, built on dhanvan, a bow, while the dhan in Dhanteras is dhana, wealth. The two share a sound, not a root, even though Dhanvantari is worshipped on the same day.

faqs.question: What is Yama Deepam and why is it done?
faqs.answer: Yama Deepam, or Yamadeepdaan, is a lamp lit outside the house at nightfall on Dhanteras in honour of Yama, the god of death. P. V. Kane records the rule from the Skanda Purana, quoted in the Nirnayamrta, and its stated purpose is to avoid accidental death in the family.

faqs.question: Which direction should the Yama Deepam face?
faqs.answer: Many families turn it to face south, the direction Hindu tradition assigns to Yama, and use an earthen lamp with four wicks. Those details come from household custom rather than the texts we read, which only say the lamp goes outside the house at nightfall.

faqs.question: Where does the King Hima story come from?
faqs.answer: We could not trace it to any Purana or older text. It is best read as a vrat katha told during the observance: a bride keeps her husband awake with lamps, gold and songs, and Yama, arriving as a snake, leaves at dawn without him.

faqs.question: Who is Dhanvantari in Hindu tradition?
faqs.answer: Dhanvantari is the physician of the gods, who rose from the churned Ocean of Milk with a bowl of amrita. The Sushruta Samhita calls him King of Kashi and presents its teaching as his, and the Ministry of Ayush describes Divodasa Dhanvantari as the head of Ayurveda's school of surgeons.

faqs.question: Is National Ayurveda Day still on Dhanteras?
faqs.answer: No. Since 2025, Ayurveda Day is fixed on 23 September every year under a Gazette notification of 23 March 2025. The last joint observance was the 9th Ayurveda Day on 29 October 2024, which the Ayush annual report says was held on Dhanvantari Jayanti.

faqs.question: Do people in Gujarat call the day Dhanteras too?
faqs.answer: Yes. P. V. Kane notes that the 13th of the dark half, the first night of Diwali, is called Dhanteras in Gujarat and Saurashtra. There it falls in Ashvin under the amanta calendar, while North Indian purnimanta calendars put the same night in Kartik.

faqs.question: Should I send a Diwali greeting on Dhanteras or wait?
faqs.answer: Either works, but most people leave festival greetings late. In SubhSandesh's Raksha Bandhan 2026 data, a small sample of 89 pages, 86.1% of on-time pages were built within 24 hours of the festival, so a Dhanteras greeting arrives early rather than late.

# Why Dhanteras Is Celebrated: Its Meaning, Stories and Yama Lamp

Why Dhanteras is celebrated comes down to three acts on one evening: honouring wealth (*dhana*), worshipping Dhanvantari, the physician of the gods, and lighting a lamp for Yama so that no one in the house dies before their time. It falls on the 13th lunar day (*teras*) of the waning moon, two days before Lakshmi Puja. If Dhanteras is also your cue to start Diwali greetings, SubhSandesh's nearest festival data comes from Raksha Bandhan 2026, a different festival and a small sample of 89 pages with a median lead time of 0 days: of the 79 finished in time, 55.7% were built on the day itself and 86.1% within 24 hours of it. This page traces each reason to the oldest text we could open, separates the "dhan" in Dhanteras from the "Dhan" in Dhanvantari, and sets out the Yama Deepam rite step by step.

## What does the word Dhanteras mean?

Dhanteras means "the wealth thirteenth": *dhan* from the Sanskrit *dhana*, wealth, and *teras*, the Hindi word for the 13th day of a lunar fortnight. Its formal name, Dhanatrayodashi, says the same thing in Sanskrit.

Both halves check out in 19th-century dictionaries. Monier-Williams's 1899 Sanskrit-English Dictionary (p. 508) glosses *dhana* first as "the prize of a contest", then as "wealth, riches, (movable) property, money, treasure". John Platts's 1884 [Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi, and English](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/platts_query.py?qs=teras&searchhws=yes) (p. 351) defines *teras* as "the thirteenth day of the lunar fortnight", reached through Prakrit from Sanskrit *trayodashi*.

The month name depends on the calendar. In the amanta reckoning used in Gujarat and Maharashtra the night is the dark 13th of Ashvin; in the purnimanta reckoning of North India it is the dark 13th of Kartik. Same night, two month names.

## Dhan is not Dhanvantari: what a 1922 study found

A popular explanation says Dhanteras is named after Dhanvantari. The dictionaries do not support it. Monier-Williams splits the god's name as [*dhanvan-tari*, "moving in a curve"](https://www.sanskrit-lexicon.uni-koeln.de/scans/csl-apidev/getword.php?dict=mw&key=Danvantari&input=slp1&output=iast), built on *dhanvan*, a bow, which is a different word from *dhana*, wealth.

Louis H. Gray, writing in the *Journal of the American Oriental Society* in 1922, called the meaning of the name "not wholly certain". In [his study of the god](https://archive.org/details/jstor-593645) he sets the bow reading aside and favours a sound-alike *dhanvan* or *dhanu*, "arid land" or "cloud", arguing that Dhanvantari began as a cloud deity who became a healer because rain revives parched land.

On either reading, the two words share a sound, not a root. Dhanteras is therefore not a renamed Dhanvantari festival: the wealth thirteenth and Dhanvantari's worship are two separate strands that came to share one night, alongside a third, the lamp for Yama.

## Three reasons Dhanteras is celebrated, oldest source first

Each strand below gets the same four facts: what it says, the oldest text we opened, its print date, and what a household does.

### 1. The lamp for Yama

The rite says a lamp lit outside the house at nightfall keeps untimely death away from the family. The oldest written form we found is a single rule: P. V. Kane's [*History of Dharmasastra*, volume V part 1](https://archive.org/details/KhistoryOfDharmasastraancientAndMediaevalReligiousAndCivilLaw) (1958, pp. 195–196), reports that the Skanda Purana, as quoted in the digest *Nirnayamrta*, provides for lighting lamps at the onset of night on the dark 13th, outside the house, in honour of Yama, "in order to avoid accidental death". A household sets one lamp at the door at dusk and leaves it there.

### 2. Dhanvantari, physician of the gods

Dhanvantari is the god who rose from the churned Ocean of Milk carrying amrita, the nectar of immortality. Gray traces his cult back to the Kaushika Sutra (74.6), which places part of the daily offering "in the water-holder for Dhanvantari", and cites the Mahabharata (1.18.38) for his rise from the ocean with a white bowl of amrita. A household offers a prayer for the family's health; Ayurvedic colleges and hospitals mark the day as Dhanvantari Jayanti.

### 3. Wealth, the house and its metal

The wealth strand asks a family to honour what it owns and ready the home for Lakshmi. Kane lists "worship of wealth" as the first of the five items of the Diwali festival and records that "before and on this day houses are painted and decorated", courtyards cleaned and "metal vessels are polished and illuminations begin"; he also cites the Padma Purana (VI.124.4) for lamps on this 13th. A household cleans, polishes its brass and steel, and lights the first lamps of Diwali.

Gray's 1922 survey, which runs from the Sutras to Punjabi folk tales, never mentions Dhanteras or any date for Dhanvantari. Read together, the texts suggest the wealth thirteenth and the Yama lamp are the older calendar fixtures, with Dhanvantari's worship joining the same night later.

## The King Hima story has no text behind it, as far as we could find

In the legend most pages lead with, a king named Hima is told his 16-year-old son will die of snakebite on the fourth night of his marriage. The bride heaps her jewellery and coins at the bedroom door, lights lamps all around, and keeps her husband awake with songs and stories; Yama arrives as a serpent, is dazzled by the glitter, sits on the heap listening till dawn, and leaves without his prize.

We could not find this story in any text we opened. Kane's account of Diwali, which cites the Skanda rule and the Padma Purana, does not mention Hima, and the top-ranking encyclopedia entry for Dhanteras sources the tale to a 2016 holiday encyclopedia, not to a Purana. The fairest reading is that it is a *vrat katha*, a story told during the observance, that dramatises the older rule: a lamp outside, and death kept from the door. It still earns its place, because it explains why gold and light sit together on this one night.

## How to do Yama Deepam on Dhanteras evening: 4 steps

Yama Deepam, also written Yamadeepdaan, is the lamp-offering to Yama. Kane's list of observances gives it in one line: on the dark 13th, "lighting lamps outside the house at night-fall; this prevents accidental death". The steps below expand that line and flag household custom.

1. **Wait for nightfall.** The rule ties the lamp to the onset of night, not to a puja muhurat. Check a local panchang for sunset in your city, because the time moves by city and by year.
2. **Place it outside.** The lamp goes outside the main door, not in the puja room; this is the one Dhanteras lamp that faces the street.
3. **Use a simple oil diya.** Many families use an earthen lamp with four wicks and turn it to face south, the direction Hindu tradition assigns to Yama. We found these details in household practice, not in the texts we read, so follow your family's custom.
4. **Name the intention.** The lamp asks for long life for everyone in the house. It is offered to Yama, not to Lakshmi, so it is not the same as the evening Lakshmi-Kubera lamps.

## The three strands compared by their evidence

The table lines up each reason for Dhanteras against the oldest source we could open and read for it.

| Strand | Oldest source we read | Printed | What it asks of a household |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lamp for Yama | Skanda Purana rule, quoted in *Nirnayamrta*, via Kane | 1958 | One lamp outside the door at nightfall |
| Dhanvantari | Kaushika Sutra 74.6 and Mahabharata 1.18.38, via Gray | 1922 | Offerings to Dhanvantari for health |
| Wealth | Kane's five-day Diwali list; Padma Purana VI.124.4 | 1958 | Clean the house, polish metal, light lamps |
| King Hima's son | No written source found | Not found | A night kept awake by lamplight |

The Yama lamp has the clearest written rule, while the story most people know has none we could trace.

## Dhanvantari Jayanti and Ayurveda Day parted after 2024

The Ministry of Ayush's [Annual Report 2024–25](https://ayush.gov.in/assets/pdf/annualReport/Annual-Report24-25_English.pdf) records the 9th Ayurveda Day on 29 October 2024 "on the occasion of Dhanvantari Jayanti", which was the last time the two shared Dhanteras. Since 2025, Ayurveda Day is fixed on 23 September every year under a Gazette notification of 23 March 2025, while Dhanvantari Jayanti stays on the dark 13th.

The same report names "Divodasa Dhanvantari" as the head of Ayurveda's school of surgeons and says the Sushruta Samhita was codified from his teaching. The [1911 Bhishagratna translation of the Sushruta Samhita](https://archive.org/details/englishtranslati00susruoft) opens its section on disease with Sushruta clasping the feet of "the holy Dhanvantari, who had arisen out of the primordial ocean with the pitcher of ambrosia on his head", and elsewhere calls him the King of Kashi.

## Sending a Dhanteras greeting, and when a link is the wrong thing

Dhanteras greetings tend to be short, and the long message usually waits for Lakshmi Puja night, two days later. The Raksha Bandhan 2026 figures above suggest most people build a festival page close to the day, so Dhanteras evening is early rather than late. Across the whole platform, 48.3% of shared pages are opened on a phone, and 90.9% of pages people start are published and shared.

For one person you want to wish properly, SubhSandesh's [interactive Diwali card with diyas, rangoli and a shagun liffafa](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-diwali) opens on a diya waiting at their door with a tag from you, then a row of wish diyas, a rangoli with your initials and sky lanterns holding up to six photos. It takes about five minutes and opens as a private link in any browser, with no app or account. If the occasion is not Diwali at all, the [full SubhSandesh template gallery](https://subhsandesh.in/templates) covers birthdays, apologies and other days.

Be clear about what it is not. It is a greeting for one person, not a puja guide or a Yama Deepam substitute; nothing on a screen replaces the lamp outside the door. For a grandparent who does not use a smartphone, a phone call on Dhanteras evening does more than any link.
